node-1.label: Episodes of continuous, low-amplitude, high-frequency jerking movements of all extremities with occasional neck and torso involvement

node-2.label: Patient is a 73-year-old woman with stage 4 chronic kidney disease and ischemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 15%-20%), presenting with acute decompensated heart failure; she was started on intravenous bumetanide and intravenous dobutamine at 2.5 mg/kg per hour.

node-3.label: Examination showed the jerking movements were generally synchronous, present both at rest and with stimulation, sometimes frequent enough to give the appearance of shivering; no fever or hypothermia was present.

why.why: Recent bumetanide and dobutamine exposure remains a competing cause, but expert analyses emphasize that the laboratory pattern (markedly elevated BUN/creatinine with normal ionized calcium and magnesium) strongly favors uremic encephalopathy. The absence of precise medication timing data prevents confirmation of drug-induced myoclonus, so confidence is reduced from 0.25 to 0.2.

Both laboratory and radiology expert analyses converge that markedly elevated BUN/creatinine, low serum sodium, normal ionized calcium and magnesium, preserved consciousness, and synchronous stimulus-sensitive myoclonus most strongly support uremic encephalopathy over electrolyte imbalance and seizure. Confidence is raised from 0.5 to 0.65; it is not higher because EEG was not obtained to confirm triphasic waves and precise drug timing/dialysis status remain unavailable.

Loop diuretic use could cause electrolyte shifts, but normal ionized calcium and magnesium on laboratory testing reduce the likelihood of electrolyte-induced myoclonus; low sodium is present but aligns more with uremic encephalopathy. Confidence is lowered to 0.1.

The clinical pattern of synchronous, stimulus-sensitive, shivering-like jerks without fever and with preserved consciousness argues against seizure; no EEG confirmatory evidence is available, and experts note subclinical seizures cannot be absolutely excluded, but seizure/status epilepticus remains unlikely. Confidence is 0.05.
